paper.disclaimer: Method note, not advice. Not a valuation report.
paper.lead: Method D is the default way we value directly held Swiss residential property. It produces a range, not a price, and it names its index and its date. This note explains the inputs, works an example, and states what the method does not do.
paper.s1_h: Why a range, not a number
paper.s1_p: A listed security has a price: the last trade on an exchange, with a time stamp. A flat does not. The only honest output of a model fed by an index and adjustment factors is a central estimate with a band around it. We show the band. A single number would imply a precision the inputs do not carry.
paper.s2_p: Four inputs. The purchase price and its date. The cantonal or municipal house-price index for the relevant segment, which moves the purchase price to today. An age factor for the building. A condition factor for the unit, set from a short checklist you fill in. The index does the heavy lifting; the factors are deliberately coarse, because a fine-grained factor would be false precision.
paper.s3_p: A Zurich apartment bought in 2016 for CHF 1,210,000. The relevant index has risen 19 percent to the latest reading, dated 12 September 2026, which gives CHF 1,440,000. An age factor of 0.99 and a condition factor of 0.99 bring the central estimate to about CHF 1,412,000. We report a band of plus or minus five percent around it, so CHF 1,412,000 to 1,548,000. The index source and its date sit beside the number in the app.
paper.s4_p: It is not a valuation report and it is not advice. It does not replace a chartered surveyor, it does not account for micro-location within a building, and it does not reflect a formal appraisal. It exists so that a large illiquid line in your net worth is not a blank, and so that the number you do show carries a method, a source and a date.
paper.s5_p: Every property line in the app shows the index name, the index date and the factors used. If the index date ages past a threshold, the value is flagged as stale rather than silently carried forward. That is the same rule the market tiles follow, and it is the rule that makes the number usable rather than decorative.

paper2.title: What the private investor rule does not cover
paper2.lead: In Switzerland a private investor pays no tax on capital gains from securities. That is the headline. This note sets out where the rule starts to bend, and why the judgment for your own situation belongs to a tax adviser, not to software.
paper2.s1_p: Under Art. 16(3) of the federal direct tax law, capital gains on privately held movable assets are not taxed. Shares, funds, bonds and crypto held as private wealth can be sold at a profit and the gain stays out of taxable income at federal level and in most cantons. Only the income the asset produces, dividends and interest, is taxed as it is paid. The gain itself is not the trigger.
paper2.s2_h: Where it stops: the professional dealer
paper2.s2_p: The same article exempts the gain only for a private investor. If the tax office reclassifies you as a professional securities dealer, the gains become taxable income and the whole exemption falls away. The Federal Tax Administration set out the test in Circular No. 36 of 27 July 2012. It looks at a bundle of habits rather than one number, and an investor who trips several of them can lose the exemption even when each habit looks modest on its own.
paper2.s3_p: Circular No. 36 weighs several factors. A holding period under six months, a trading volume above five times the portfolio at the start of the year, gains that make up more than half of net income, leverage, and heavy use of derivatives all count against you. A clean private investor tends to hold longer than six months, trades well under five times the portfolio, keeps gains below half of income, and does not run the book on borrowed money. These are the safe-harbour markers the Administration describes, not a formula that guarantees a result.
paper2.s4_h: Two cases the rule never covers
paper2.s4_p: Two things sit outside the exemption no matter how patient you are. A gain on Swiss real estate is always taxed, through the cantonal real-estate gains tax (Grundstückgewinnsteuer), which is separate from income tax and has its own rates and holding-period relief. Employee shares and options carry their own rules, and a discount at grant can be taxed as income long before you sell. And the assets themselves still feed the annual wealth tax, which is levied on the holding whether or not it ever produces a gain.
paper2.s5_p: The app can show you a realized gain and its holding period. It can flag a position held under six months, or a year where disposals ran high against the portfolio. What it cannot do is decide whether your pattern of trades crosses into professional dealing, because that is a judgment on your whole situation, not a lookup. That call belongs to your tax adviser. We mark the flag and hand you the evidence.
paper2.disclaimer: Tax information, not tax advice. The classification of a private investor is a judgment for your adviser. See Art. 16(3) DBG and FTA Circular No. 36 of 27 July 2012.
